idiom_name: pthread worker pool over a part queue + completion counter + merge
implementation_notes: C has no future, channel or aggregation primitive, so the composite is built from pthreads: the splitter walks the composite and enqueues one work item per part - each carrying the correlation key, part index and count, and an owned payload buffer - into a mutex-protected queue; a fixed worker pool pops items, dispatches on the part kind through a function-pointer table, and writes results into the per-composite slot array. Completion is decided by a shared counter (a mutex or C11 atomic): the last writer performs the merge and hands the assembled message to the next stage. The classic structure is not optional here, so the only real design choices are the dispatcher (function-pointer table versus switch) and whether the completion counter is guarded by the queue mutex or its own lock.
pitfalls: pthread_join on every part thread destroys the pool's benefit: join the pool at shutdown and signal completion through the aggregator's counter instead.
The completion counter and result slots are shared mutable state; without a mutex or C11 atomics the last-writer test tears and the merge either never runs or runs twice.
The work item must own its payload (copy or explicit ownership transfer); a pool that keeps pointers into the composite message reads freed memory once the split loop moves on.
